description: I am a passionate problem-solver and tech enthusiast skilled in data analysis and rapid prototyping, eager to tackle real-world space and Earth challenges using NASA’s open data. Joining my team means collaborating on creative, high-impact ideas with strong drive and clear communication. I am currently looking for teammates with skills in UI/UX design, software development, and machine learning to build a complete project.
summary:
Spacewise is an Earth Jukebox that lets people hear NASA Earth Information Center visualizations instead of only seeing them. Built with React and the Web Audio API, it plays three EIC videos (global temperature anomalies, carbon dioxide plumes, and Arctic sea ice minimum) and analyzes each frame in real time. Pixel colors are turned into a signal: warm reds for temperature, bright plumes for CO2, and white pixels for sea ice, where shrinking ice raises the pitch. That signal drives a synthesizer locked to a C-minor pentatonic scale, so the result stays musical, and stereo panning follows where the signal sits from west to east.

Accessibility is central. Playback, track switching and seeking all work from the keyboard, timestamped milestones and an audio legend are read aloud with speech synthesis, and status updates are announced to screen readers. The app runs fully offline from bundled videos, so it works without a connection. Spacewise matters because it opens Earth science to blind and low-vision users and gives everyone a new, emotional way to feel climate change.
details:
What it does: Spacewise is an Earth Jukebox that turns NASA Earth Information Center visualizations into sound as they play. The user picks one of three videos (global temperature anomalies, carbon dioxide plumes, or the Arctic sea ice minimum) and presses Space. Every video frame is drawn to a hidden canvas and analyzed in real time. The result is a signal for how strong the feature is and where it sits horizontally. That signal drives a synthesizer, so the user hears the data change as the visualization changes.

How the translation works: For temperature, warmth is red minus blue, so deep bass means cooler years and high chimes mean extreme warming. For CO2, bright red, orange and yellow pixels mark plumes, and pitch rises with concentration. For sea ice, white pixels count as ice and the mapping is inverted, so low grounded tones mean thick ice and the pitch rises as ice shrinks. The sound pans left to right to follow where the signal is on the map, from west to east. Notes come from a C-minor pentatonic scale spanning C3 to G5, so the output stays musical.

Accessibility and benefits: Blind and low-vision users can follow Earth science that is normally shown only as pictures. Playback, track switching, an audio legend and seeking all work from the keyboard. Timestamped milestones and the legend are read aloud with speech synthesis, and status changes are announced to screen readers. The app runs fully offline from bundled videos, so it still works at an event or in a classroom with poor internet.

Intended impact: To make climate data something people can experience as well as read, for accessibility and for emotional connection. Hearing ice loss or rising heat as rising pitch makes the scale of change easier to grasp.

Tools: JavaScript with React 19 and Vite for the interface. The Web Audio API (oscillators, gain and stereo panner) makes the sound, the Canvas 2D API reads the frames, and the Web Speech API provides the narration. A small Node.js Express server is in place for future live NASA data. We used ESLint and Git/GitHub. The only hardware needed is a computer with a browser and speakers or headphones.

Creativity: The signal’s horizontal position sets the stereo pan, so the sound follows the map. The sea ice track uses an inverse mapping, because the loss is the story. The voice narrator is part of the instrument, so users get context as well as sound.

Factors we considered: Accessibility came first, so we did not rely on sight for any control. We kept the sound musical rather than noisy. We sampled every 16th pixel to keep analysis fast enough for real-time playback. We made it offline-first so the demo does not depend on a connection. One limit is that the analysis reads the colors in the video, not the underlying data values. Using the raw datasets and testing with blind and low-vision users are our next steps.
